definition: Pages are a new document format announced at OpenAI's DevDay 2026, built so that people and AI agents can co-author the same document. A Page can hold text, images, and charts, and — the key difference from a normal doc — an agent can be invited in as a co-author: drafting sections, generating charts from data, illustrating ideas. They are designed to live inside ChatGPT Space, the shared workspace, alongside full apps built by third-party developers (“plugin extensions”).

edges.label: built for agentic co-authorship
edges.note: Pages assume the author may be software — the document is a shared surface between you and an agent.

edges.label: agent co-author needs data rules
edges.note: An agent that writes in your documents needs the same per-role access rules as any tool user.

example.body: You're writing the quarterly business review. You write the narrative; your dot reads the sales database, generates the bar charts, and drafts the “key takeaways” section overnight. You wake up to a Page that is 70% drafted — you edit, correct one chart's numbers, and publish. The document holds both kinds of authorship in one place, which is exactly why the finished page should say which parts came from the machine.
example.title: The quarterly review, co-written

name: Pages
tagline: Documents built for humans and AI agents to write, chart, and illustrate together.
whyItMatters: Documents have always been human-authored, with AI as a helper. Pages flip that: the document becomes a shared surface between you and an agent. That's powerful for reports and decks — and it raises a plain question worth asking of any co-authored page: which parts did the human write, and which came from the machine?
